name: McBling

image.caption: McBling Saturday Night candle with glitter and a disco ball, very Gen Z, unknown designer, produced by DW Home, circa 2024, glass and wax, sold at T•J•maxx in Miami, US (01)

lead: McBling is a name for the maximalist fashion and beauty style of roughly 2000 to 2008: rhinestones, velour tracksuits, low-rise jeans, lots of pink, shiny accessories and brand logos. It was shaped by celebrity tabloid culture and reality TV, with figures such as Paris Hilton and Nicole Richie often cited.

The term was coined retrospectively, in 2017, by Froyo Tam of the Consumer Aesthetics Research Institute during a Facebook poll. In recent years it has been revived among Gen Z through thrifting and brand relaunches, and is often mislabelled as Y2K.

paras: People recreate it with bedazzled or sequined pieces, matching tracksuits, oversized sunglasses, large handbags and bright, glossy or glittery makeup, often found by thrifting vintage items.
It is a clothing and styling choice with no health concerns beyond the usual ones for cosmetics and accessories, such as skin sensitivity to products.

angle.text: People adopt McBling to look deliberately glamorous: bedazzled clothes, gloss and glitter, big accessories. It changes how an outfit and overall styling read rather than bodily features.

lead: McBling is a fashion and lifestyle aesthetic associated with roughly 2003 to 2008, defined by a more-is-more approach: bedazzled clothing, velour tracksuits, low-rise jeans, graphic tees, pink, oversized sunglasses and visible luxury logos from labels such as Juicy Couture, Von Dutch and Baby Phat.[1] People use it as a way to look openly glamorous and playful.

The name was coined on 5 January 2017 by Froyo Tam of the Consumer Aesthetics Research Institute in a poll run by Evan Collins, combining the McDonald's prefix Mc with bling.[1] It is distinguished from Y2K futurism, which favoured silvers and cool blues, whereas McBling favoured pinks, golds and sparkle and drew on tabloid celebrity culture, reality TV and MySpace.[1] It declined with the 2008 recession and has since returned through Gen Z nostalgia, thrifting and brand relaunches.[1]
infobox: Paris Hilton, Nicole Richie, Britney Spears[1]

paras: Hallmarks include bedazzled tops and phones, sequins, matching sets, mini skirts, large designer bags and a pink-heavy palette.[1]

It emerged in a period of tabloid celebrity culture and conspicuous consumption, and was shaped by hip-hop figures such as Missy Elliott and LL Cool J who popularised matching sets.[1] Revival figures cited include Ice Spice and Bella Hadid.[1]

timeline.event: Aesthetic emerges as a recognisable style.[1]
